title: Chapter 155 – A Bronze Door in the Cold
html:
[The Sky Wall – Lin Jian]

The foothills of the Sky Wall are not hills at all. They are the broken teeth of something that fell a very long time ago, and the silver road climbs through them like a thread through the eye of a needle.

By the ninth day the grass has gone. There is bare scree and black rock and the dull glitter of frozen streams, and above it, filling the whole northern sky, the Wall itself: not a range of mountains but a single sheer rampart, blue-white and appalling, with cliffs so high that the tops are lost in cloud. Jian has to tip his head back to see the notch. It is still there, a small dark cleft, a long way up. It has not grown closer in two days. It looks like a mouth that is not yet ready to speak.

He walks with his staff in his right hand and his left hand pressed flat against his chest, over the Core. It is a habit he has fallen into without noticing. The gold is warm. It hums in time with the road. On the worst stretches, where the silver line runs thin and he must fold the gap, he feels it like a tendon pulled too tight. Bell has stopped writing in her notebook. She no longer has to; she knows his hands by heart.

"How are the knees?" she says, behind him.

"I am eighty-seven."

"That is not an answer."

"They are old." He glances back. She is blue-lipped with cold, wrapped to the eyes in a wool scarf, and still she is smiling at him with grim professional patience. "They are older than they were. Is that a better answer?"

"It is a more honest one." She hitches her satchel. "We stop at the next flat place. Do not argue."

He does not argue. He has learned.

* * *

The first beast they see is dead.

It lies beside the road at the foot of a boulder, frozen solid, a horned wolf the size of a pony. Its pelt is white and gray and shaggy. Its horns, two curved spikes of black bone as long as Jian's arm, are sheathed in rime. Its eyes are open, filmed over, staring at nothing. There is no wound on it. There is no sign of a fight. It has simply lain down in the snow, in the middle of its journey, and died of cold or of running or of something else.

"Rank two," says Bell, kneeling. She has pulled off a glove and laid two fingers against the cold throat. "At least. See the gland under the jaw? That is a sign. It has a core."

"Is it dangerous?"

"Not now." She stands. Her face is pale. "I have read about these. The old herbals. The horn is good for fevers. The liver is a violent poison. I have never seen one." She looks around. "There will be more."

There are. They find the second a mile on, and the third and fourth a little farther, sprawled along the road in the lee of the rocks like drifts of gray snow. A great elk, antlers frozen into the ice. A pair of bears, locked in an embrace of death, with frost on their lashes. A hundred small things, hares and foxes and marmots, trodden into the ground. The scree is a shambles of tracks. They overlap in a vast trampled mass, as if a river of animals had poured past in the night and left the weak behind.

They were running, says the boy, very quietly. All of them. From something behind.

Or toward something in front.

Which?

He does not know. He stands in the road with his hand on his chest, listening, and the Wall stands over him, blue and silent, and the wind carries a thin high cry from somewhere far above, long and trembling, like a child calling in the dark.

* * *

The second beast is alive.

He does not see it until the sun is going down. They have made camp, such as it is, in the lee of a boulder, with a small oil stove and a sheet of oiled canvas pegged against the wind. Bell is boiling rice. Yue is sitting cross-legged with her palms on the ground, listening. Pebble sits on her shoulder, very still.

And on the ridge above the camp, silhouetted against the red sky, something is watching them.

It is huge. That is the first thing. It is the size of a small house, white as milk, crouched on the rim of the rocks with its great paws hanging over the edge like a cat on a wall. It has the body of a lion and the head of something older, broad and flat and noble, with a mane that stirs in the wind like frozen smoke. Its eyes are the color of wet slate. It is looking straight at him.

He rises, slowly. His heart is beating in his throat.

"Don't move," he says. He does not have to; nobody has. Bell has stopped stirring the pot. Yue has lifted her head. Between them, the oil stove ticks and hisses.

Snow-lion, whispers the boy. Rank three. It's on the old maps. It's not supposed to be this far down.

Can you read it?

No. It's... it's very quiet. A pause. Brother. It isn't angry.

The beast lifts its head. It opens its mouth, and a sound comes out of it, a deep slow rumbling thrum that Jian feels in his ribs. It is not a roar. It is closer to a purr, or a word. He cannot tell. Beside him Yue has gone rigid. Her eyes are closed. Her hand has found his sleeve.

Then Pebble leaps down from her shoulder.

He lands lightly on the frozen ground, a small gray shape with a pale line down his back, and trots out into the open. He does not hurry. He goes to the foot of the rocks and sits down and tilts his head back, and the two of them regard each other across fifty feet of dusk: the stone and the lion, the cracked back and the white mane.

The snow-lion lowers its great head, slowly, until its chin is on the rock between its paws.

It is a bow.

For a long moment no one moves. Then the beast rises, shakes the rime from its pelt in a long rippling shiver, and turns away. It pads along the ridge without a sound, and the dusk takes it. Where it stood there is only a patch of bare black stone and a few drifting flakes.

"What," says Bell faintly, "was that?"

That, says Pebble, in his deep dry voice, to all of them at once, was the oldest friend I have.

* * *

He tells it by the stove, in a low shaken voice, with his cracked back to the light.

I have not told you everything. I did not know how. It came back slowly, as the key turned. First the door. Then the hand. Then the words. His black eyes glint. And now I remember the lion.

She was a cub, he goes on. On the day he left me. A tiny white thing, no bigger than I am, wet from the snow. He found her in the cliff, abandoned, and set her beside me at the foot of the door. He said: look after her. Look after each other. Wait for the gardener.

Ethan, says the boy.

Ethan. The little voice cracks. He was always tired. He always smelled of tea and smoke. I do not think he had slept for a hundred years. He set me down at the door with his scarred hand on my back, and he said, I am sorry for the cold. A pause. And then he walked into the dark, and the door closed, and the snow came down.

Nobody speaks. Beyond the canvas the wind picks up. The stove hisses.

We waited, says Pebble. Both of us. For a long time. The cub grew. I did not. One winter she said, I think I will go and look. And she went up the cliff, and I did not see her again. He turns his head toward the ridge where the white shape stood. I did not think she would remember.

She remembered you, says Yue, with her hands. Tears are on her face.

She did. The voice is wondering. She has not stopped waiting, either.

Jian looks into the fire. The coals are red and shifting. He thinks of seven children asleep in a hall. He thinks of a stone and a cub at the foot of a bronze door in the snow. Everything that has ever been left behind seems to be waiting somewhere in the cold, he thinks, patient and uncomplaining, for a hand that does not come.

I'm glad we came, says the boy, in the room.

So am I.

* * *

The avalanche comes on the tenth morning.

They are a mile into the canyon, in single file, and Jian is counting steps, when the silver road gives a lurch under his boots like a living thing. Yue, ahead of him, stops dead with her arms thrown wide. She cannot hear it; she feels it in her soles. A deep slow grinding shudder is going through the rock. High above, the strip of pale sky between the cliffs has gone strangely still.

Then the ice lets go.

It does not fall. It pours. A whole shoulder of the north wall, blue and white and thousands of tons, breaks free with a sound like the end of the world, and comes down the canyon in a roaring white wall that fills the slot from side to side. He sees it as one sees a nightmare, far off and very clear. He sees Bell's mouth open on a scream he cannot hear. He sees Yue turn, too late, with her hand reaching for her satchel.

Fold! cries the boy.

There is no time for thought. He plants his staff, and drops into the Core as a man drops into cold water, and takes hold of the road with all the gold in his chest, and the silver line under his feet wrinkles. It folds. He feels it do it. Forty paces of canyon floor, with the three of them in it, creased in half like a cloth, and then, with a lurch that turns his stomach, they are standing a hundred yards up the slot, on the far side of a boulder as big as a barn.

The avalanche goes past.

It takes the place where they stood. It roars on down the canyon in a boiling cloud of white, and the air fills with powder and thunder. Snow rains down on his shoulders. Bell is on her knees with her scarf over her face. Yue is clutching his arm so hard that her nails have gone through the cloth. The echoes roll away down the valley, getting fainter and fainter, and then there is only the hiss of settling ice and, very far off, the cry of a bird.

He stands there swaying. His chest is a hot knot. When he looks at his hands, they are shaking like leaves, and the skin on the back is thin and creased and spotted as a very old man's.

"Five," says Bell, in a whisper. She has crawled over to him and has two fingers on his wrist. "That was five steps in one fold. Five hairs at least. Maybe a month. Maybe two." Her voice cracks. "Jian. Please tell me you are all right."

"I am alive."

"That is not what I asked."

"I know." He tries to smile. "I am tired, Bell. I am very tired. But I would do it again."

She stares at him. Then, with a ferocity that startles him, she throws her arms around his neck and holds on.

* * *

That night the boy asks him a question in the dark.

They are lying side by side in the lee of the boulder, wrapped in blankets, with the stove turned low. Bell is asleep, snoring faintly. Yue is awake; he can see the gleam of her open eyes. She has Pebble tucked inside her cloak against her chest, and she has not let go of him since the lion.

Brother? says the boy.

Yes.

What if I say it wrong?

He turns his head. In the room, the boy is sitting at the round table with his hands in his lap, small and straight in his white shirt. He has not touched the tea.

Say what?

The answer. For the door. A pause. Pebble says it's a question. One question. And if I say the wrong thing, it won't open. And then Pebble will have waited for nothing.

You will not say the wrong thing.

You don't know that.

No. He considers. But I know you. You are the one who gave me your name when I did not have one. You do not say wrong things. You say true ones.

That's not the same.

It is, in the end. Jian looks up at the stars, sharp and cold in the narrow strip of sky. I think the door is not asking for a clever answer. I think it is asking what you do. And you already know.

Do I?

Think of the Garden.

The boy is silent for a long time. The stove ticks. Far away, high on the cliff, something calls, a long falling cry.

I guess, says the boy slowly, I just look after people.

Yes.

That's a boring answer.

It is the best one there is. Jian smiles into the dark. Go to sleep.

* * *

They reach the door on the eleventh day.

The notch is not a notch. It is a canyon, narrow and sheer, a long blue slot cut in the face of the Wall, with walls of black ice rising on either side to a strip of pale sky. The silver road runs up the middle of it, a bright thread on the frozen floor. The wind that blows down it is steady and bitter and smells of iron. At the end, where the canyon closes into a blind rocky corner, stands the door.

It is bronze.

Jian had imagined something grand. It is not. It is a plain slab of green-black metal, perhaps twelve feet high, set into the living rock like a window into a mountain. There is no handle. There is no lock. There is a single hand-shaped hollow in the center of it at about the height of his heart, worn bright with use, and below it, scratched into the surface with a nail, a seven-fold spiral.

He stands before it for a long time with the snow drifting around his boots.

That's the one, whispers the boy. The one I saw. In the corridor.

Yes.

It's smaller than I thought.

So was the Gate. He steps forward. His hand, white-haired and veined, a little spotted, comes up on its own. The palm hovers an inch above the hollow. He can feel it humming. It is the same note as the road, but lower, and not alone. Behind it, deep in the metal, a second note is rising to meet him.

"Wait," says Pebble.

He is at Jian's feet. He has not moved so quickly since the siege. His small gray form is rigid, and his back, where the crack runs, has begun to glow a pale and trembling white.

It will not open for you. Not yet. His voice is strained. It was not made for a Keeper. It was made for a gardener. It will ask you a question, and you must answer it, and I do not know what the question is.

"Ethan did not leave you a hint?"

He left me the door. A strange noise comes from the creature, a dry little laugh. He was not a man for hints.

Jian looks at the hollow. He looks at his hand. Then, with a breath, he lays it flat on the bronze.

* * *

The door speaks.

It is a man's voice. Mild. Weary. Very slightly embarrassed, the voice of someone recording a message at three in the morning and wondering whether anyone will ever hear it. It comes from the metal, from the rock, from the air itself, and it is close enough that the hair rises on his arms.

Hello. This is a recording. If you're hearing it, the door has been tripped, which means somebody has laid a hand on the plate who is not me. That's good. That's what I hoped. Please don't be alarmed.

The sixth door is not a lock. I'm sorry about the cold; I couldn't find anywhere better. It's a question. One question. I'd like you to answer it honestly, because if you don't, I'll know, and I won't be able to help it. It's built that way. I don't like it either.

Here it is.

Gardener. State your work.

Silence. The wind moans down the canyon. Jian stands with his palm on the bronze, frozen, and the question hangs in the cold air like smoke.

State your work.

He thinks of the Keeper's oath. He thinks of the Roll, the Dock, the Seat; of the Core burning in his chest; of the long road and its cost. All of it is true, and none of it is an answer. I keep. I read. I wake. They are the words of a servant. They are what the Order would say.

Brother, says the boy.

I don't know what to say.

I do.

Say it.

No. The small voice is certain. You have to let me.

For a moment Jian does not understand. Then he does. He draws a breath, and shuts his eyes, and lets go.

It is the easiest thing in the world. The boy is there, at the front of his mind, small and straight and perfectly calm, and he lifts the old white-haired hand and keeps it flat on the bronze, and says, in a high clear voice that echoes down the frozen canyon:

"I tend a family."

The door is silent.

"I don't know what else I am. I don't know what a gardener is. But there's a tree, and I grew up under it. There's a house with a kitchen. There are a lot of people in it, and they eat too much and talk too loud and they're all mine. I look after them. That's all I do." His voice shakes. "And when somebody gets lost, I go and get them. That's my work."

A long pause.

Thank you, says the recording. That's it. That's all I wanted to hear.

Please come in.

* * *

The metal moves.

It does not swing. It does not slide. It opens, like an eye, the green-black surface thinning from the center outward into a circle of clear amber light, and the cold goes out of the air, all at once, like a held breath. A warm dry wind comes through, smelling of dust and rain and cut grass. Bell cries out. Yue has fallen to her knees.

And Pebble is screaming.

It is not a sound. It is a pressure, a high white terrible note that goes through Jian's skull like a nail. The little creature has thrown himself against the bronze. His back is split from nape to tail, and light is pouring out of the crack, not pale now but molten, a gold so bright that it hurts to look at. His four feet scrabble on the frozen ground. His black eyes are wide.

I am the key, he says. It needs me. It needs the key to stay in the lock. It won't hold unless—

"Pebble!"

Let me. He is shaking all over. It is not a bad thing. It is what I was made for. I just did not know it would hurt.

"No. We'll find another way—"

There is none. The voice is very faint. Let me do this one thing, Jian. Let me hold it open.

Yue is beside him already. She has thrown herself down on the frozen ground with her arms around the little gray body, and her face is wet and distorted and furious. She is signing, wildly, with her cheek against the stone. He cannot read it. He doesn't need to.

I know, says Pebble to her. I know. I'll come back. I'm only going to be quiet.

You promised.

I did. I always keep them.

The light pours out of him. It fills the doorway. It pours into the amber circle, and the bronze rings once, deep and low, like a bell struck underwater, and the door stands open on a long bright hall.

And then the creature goes limp in Yue's arms.

* * *

For a long time nobody speaks.

Yue sits on the ground with the little body cradled against her chest. His eyes are closed. His breathing is slow, so slow that Bell has to put her ear to his side to be sure. The crack in his back has closed, a little, and the glow is gone; he is simply a small gray stone creature, cold, heavy, ordinary. He feels, Jian thinks, like a river pebble. He does not feel like anything alive.

"He's breathing," says Bell, hoarsely. "He is. It is very slow. I think... I think he's sleeping."

Yue's hands move. They are shaking. Bell watches and shakes her head, helplessly.

"I don't know what she's saying."

Jian does. He kneels and takes his sister's face in both his hands, and she looks at him, and he sees what she is trying to say. It is the first time in thirteen years that no voice has come into her head. The deep dry friendly murmur that has translated her whole life since the day she took the jar is gone. She cannot hear Bell. She cannot hear him. She cannot hear the wind or the snow or the groan of the open door.

She is, for the first time, entirely deaf.

He takes the slate from his pack. Temur's slate, worn smooth by a boy's thumbs. He wipes it with his sleeve. Then he takes a stub of chalk, and in large clear letters, slowly, writes:

He is not dead. He is holding the door. He will wake when we come home.

She reads it. She reads it again. Her mouth works. She hugs the stone creature to her chest and bends over him, rocking.

Behind them the bronze door stands open on its long warm hall, bright with amber light, and the wind from the other world blows over the three of them like a hand on a child's hair. Jian looks into it. He thinks of a small gray shape on a black ledge at the foot of a bronze door in the snow, waiting, and of the six hundred years he gave.

Thank you, he thinks.

He heard, says the boy, from the room. I think.

He rises. He helps his sister to her feet. Bell takes her other arm. And together, slowly, carrying the sleeping stone between them, they step across the threshold into the light.

Behind them the bronze door does not close. It holds, as the little stone in Yue's arms holds, quiet and patient, an eye left open in a dark wall. Ahead of them, the hall runs on into a distance that has no end: smooth floor of pale stone, walls of soft light, and a ceiling so high and so even that it might be the sky of another world. Far down it, very small, a figure in a white gown stands waiting with its hands folded.

Jian lifts his staff and walks to meet it. Beside him, his sister walks in silence, and Bell, holding her satchel to her chest, whispers a word he has never heard her say in her life.

"Please."

Nobody asks her what she means.
